title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with Neural Networks
text:
Approach
All work in this project was implemented in Python 3.12.3. Datasets underwent preprocessing and EDA using pandas (v2.2.3). Irrelevant columns and high cardinality features were removed. “Date of Birth” was transformed into “Age.” Columns with >50% missing data were dropped. Ordinal encoding was applied to the column with ordinal data using scikit-learn (v1.6.1) (Pedregosa et al., 2011). Absence counts were binned into categories. One-hot encoding was used for other categorical features. Missing values were addressed by removing observations when the fraction of NAs was below 2%. When needed, feature engineering techniques were applied to create new features that provided additional insights. NumPy (v1.26.4) was used for numerical computations.

Dataset Progression
The original work was performed using a progressive approach, where the dataset was successively enriched to evaluate how additional information impacts model performance:

Stage 1: Core student profiles
Stage 2: Engagement metrics were added to the dataset.
Stage 3: Academic performance metrics were added to the dataset.

Here I show only some of the relevant steps and results from Stage 3, for demonstration purposes.


Methodology

Preprocessing: Following an initial EDA phase to better understand the dataset, data encoding, scaling, and feature engineering were performed. Specific steps included:

Remove columns not useful in the analysis.
Remove columns with high cardinality (use >200 unique values, as a guideline for this data set).
Remove columns with >50% missing values.
Perform ordinal encoding for ordinal data.
Perform one-hot encoding for all other categorical data.
Choose how to engage with rows that have missing values, which can be done in one of two ways for this project:

Impute the rows with appropriate values.
Remove rows with missing values but ONLY in cases where rows with missing values are minimal: <2% of the overall data.


Model: Neural Network with hyperparameter tuning
Evaluation: ROC-AUC with hyperparameter tuning, learning curves, and confusion matrices
Evaluation: ROC-AUC, F1-score, precision-recall metrics
Comparison: Performance analysis across all three data stages

Neural Network Model Development:
Neural networks were built using TensorFlow (v2.19.0) and Keras (v3.10.0) with architectures spanning 1-3 hidden layers (16-128 units each), ReLU activation functions, and Softmax output layers. Regularization techniques included Dropout (0.2-0.3) and L1/L2 penalties to prevent overfitting. Models employed Adam or RMSProp optimizers with learning rates ranging from 0.01 to 0.001, paired with sparse categorical crossentropy loss. Early stopping (patience=3) and deterministic batch shuffling ensured both generalization and reproducibility across training runs.
The development process began with comprehensive environment configuration to suppress TensorFlow logging artifacts (TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL=3) and disable oneDNN optimization warnings. Feature matrices (X) were constructed by isolating the target variable (y=‘CompletedCourse_Yes’) from the dataset, followed by a nested train-test split strategy: an initial 80-20 split created validation sets, then a secondary 80-20 split of remaining training data generated test sets. This three-way partitioning enabled robust model selection via the validation set while preserving an untouched test set for final evaluation.
Data preprocessing employed StandardScaler for feature normalization across all splits. Post-scaling validation confirmed zero NaN/Inf values—a critical checkpoint before model training. Unique sample counts were verified across splits to detect potential data leakage or duplication issues that could artificially inflate performance metrics. Target variable distribution analysis across all three splits verified balanced class representation, addressing concerns inherent to imbalanced classification tasks.

Construction of the Neural Network Model
The implementation architecture centered on deterministic training through set_global_determinism(), which configured environment variables (PYTHONHASHSEED, TF_DETERMINISTIC_OPS, TF_CUDNN_DETERMINISTIC) and enabled TensorFlow’s experimental operation determinism. This framework guaranteed reproducible results across training runs—essential for scientific validity and model comparison.
The create_model() function employed strategic seeding with GlorotUniform kernel initialization and Zeros bias initialization, both parameterized with model-specific seeds. Nine architectural configurations were systematically tested, spanning 1-3 hidden layers with 16-64 units per layer. Each configuration received a unique deterministic seed (42+i) to ensure independent yet reproducible training trajectories.
The train_models_deterministic() orchestrator managed training loops with session clearing (tf.keras.backend.clear_session()) and garbage collection between model iterations to prevent memory accumulation. Models trained for 50 epochs maximum with batch_size=32 and deterministic shuffling enabled. Early stopping monitored validation loss with patience=3, automatically restoring optimal weights. Training histories captured loss/accuracy trajectories for both training and validation sets, alongside final performance metrics and seed values for complete experimental traceability.

# Suppress TensorFlow warnings and logs
os.environ['TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL'] = '3'  # Suppress all TF logs (0=all, 1=info, 2=warning, 3=error)
os.environ['TF_ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPTS'] = '0'  # Disable oneDNN optimizations warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

# Additional TensorFlow logging suppression
tf.get_logger().setLevel('ERROR')
tf.autograph.set_verbosity(0)

def set_global_determinism(seed=42):
    """
    Enable 100% reproducibility on operations related to tensor and randomness.
    """
    os.environ['PYTHONHASHSEED'] = str(seed)
    os.environ['TF_DETERMINISTIC_OPS'] = '1'
    os.environ['TF_CUDNN_DETERMINISTIC'] = '1'
    
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    tf.random.set_seed(seed)
    
    # Configure TensorFlow for determinism
    tf.config.experimental.enable_op_determinism()

# Call this at the very beginning of your script
set_global_determinism(42)

# Define Baseline Model with seed reset
def create_model(input_dim, output_dim, layers=2, units=128, dropout=0.2, lr=0.001, seed=42):
    # Reset seeds before each model creation
    tf.random.set_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    
    model = Sequential(name=f"model_{layers}L_{units}U")
    model.add(InputLayer(shape=(input_dim,)))
    
    for _ in range(layers):
        model.add(Dense(units, activation='relu', 
                       kernel_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.GlorotUniform(seed=seed),
                       bias_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.Zeros()))
        model.add(Dropout(dropout, seed=seed))
    
    model.add(Dense(output_dim, activation='softmax',
                   kernel_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.GlorotUniform(seed=seed),
                   bias_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.Zeros()))
    
    model.compile(optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=lr),
                 loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
                 metrics=['accuracy'])
    return model

# Training setup with deterministic seeds
def train_models_deterministic(architecture_configs, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val):
    models_base_s3 = []
    histories_base_s3 = []
    
    for i, config in enumerate(architecture_configs):
        print(f"\nTraining Model {i+1}: {config}")
        
        # Set unique but deterministic seed for each model
        model_seed = 42 + i
        set_global_determinism(model_seed)
        
        # Clear session
        tf.keras.backend.clear_session()
        gc.collect()
        
        # Create model with specific seed
        model = create_model(input_dim, output_dim, seed=model_seed, **config)
        
        # Early stopping
        early_stop = EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=3, 
                                 restore_best_weights=True)
        
        # Train with deterministic batch shuffling
        history = model.fit(X_train, y_train,
                          validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
                          batch_size=32,
                          epochs=50,
                          callbacks=[early_stop],
                          shuffle=True,  # This will be deterministic due to seed
                          verbose=0)
        
        # Evaluate
        train_loss, train_accuracy = model.evaluate(X_train, y_train, verbose=0)
        val_loss, val_acc = model.evaluate(X_val, y_val, verbose=0)
        
        # Store results
        models_base_s3.append(model)
        histories_base_s3.append({
            "config": config,
            "train_loss": train_loss,
            "train_accuracy": train_accuracy,
            "val_loss": val_loss,
            "val_accuracy": val_acc,
            "history": history,
            "seed": model_seed
        })
        
        print(f"Final validation accuracy: {val_acc:.4f}")
        gc.collect()
    
    return models_base_s3, histories_base_s3

# Usage
set_global_determinism(42)  # Set at the beginning

# Get dimensions
input_dim = X_train_scaled_s3.shape[1]
output_dim = len(np.unique(y_train_s3))

# --- Evaluation Function ---
# Set random seeds for reproducibility

def evaluate_trained_models(models, hist_metrics, X_test, y_test, 
                           class_names=None, verbose=True, return_curves=False):
    """
    Comprehensive model evaluation function optimized for imbalanced datasets
    
    Parameters:
    -----------
    models : list
        List of trained Keras models
    hist_metrics : list
        List of training history and config data
    X_test : array-like
        Test features
    y_test : array-like

        Whether to return ROC and PR curve data
    
    Returns:
    --------
    results : list
        Comprehensive evaluation results for each model
    """
    
    # Set seeds for reproducible evaluation
    np.random.seed(42)
    
    results_base_s3 = []
    n_classes = len(np.unique(y_test))
    is_binary = n_classes == 2
    
    if verbose:
        print("="*80)
        print(f"EVALUATING {len(models)} MODELS ON TEST SET")
        print(f"Dataset: {len(y_test)} samples, {n_classes} classes")
        if is_binary:
            class_dist = np.bincount(y_test)
            print(f"Class distribution: {class_dist[0]}:{class_dist[1]} ({class_dist[1]/len(y_test)*100:.1f}% positive)")
        print("="*80)
    
    for i, (model, history_data) in enumerate(zip(models, hist_metrics)):
        config = history_data['config']
        model_name = f"Model_{i+1}_{config['layers']}L_{config['units']}U"
        
        if verbose:
            print(f"\n{model_name}")
            print("-" * 50)
        
        try:
            # Get predictions - CONSISTENT APPROACH
            y_pred_prob = model.predict(X_test, verbose=0)
            
            # FIXED: Consistent probability extraction
            if y_pred_prob.shape[1] > 1:  # Multi-class output
                y_pred_class = np.argmax(y_pred_prob, axis=1)
                if is_binary:
                    # For binary classification, use probability of positive class (class 1)
                    y_prob_positive = y_pred_prob[:, 1]
                else:
                    y_prob_positive = y_pred_prob  # Keep all probabilities for multi-class
            else:  # Single output (sigmoid activation)
                y_pred_prob = y_pred_prob.flatten()
                y_pred_class = (y_pred_prob > 0.5).astype(int)
                y_prob_positive = y_pred_prob
            
            # Basic metrics
            test_loss, test_accuracy = model.evaluate(X_test, y_test, verbose=0)
            
            # Classification metrics
            if is_binary:
                # Binary classification metrics
                precision = precision_score(y_test, y_pred_class, zero_division=0)
                recall = recall_score(y_test, y_pred_class, zero_division=0)
                f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred_class, zero_division=0)
                
                # Class-specific metrics
                precision_per_class = precision_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                recall_per_class = recall_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                f1_per_class = f1_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                
                # FIXED: Use consistent function for ROC-AUC calculation
                roc_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob_positive)
                
                # Alternative calculation using roc_curve + auc (should match)
                fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, y_prob_positive)
                roc_auc_manual = auc(fpr, tpr)
                
                # Precision-Recall AUC (better for imbalanced data)
                precision_curve, recall_curve, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_test, y_prob_positive)
                pr_auc = auc(recall_curve, precision_curve)
                
                # Confusion matrix components
                cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_class)
                tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()
                
                # Additional metrics for imbalanced data
                specificity = tn / (tn + fp) if (tn + fp) > 0 else 0
                sensitivity = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0  # Same as recall
                
                # Matthews Correlation Coefficient (good for imbalanced data)
                mcc = ((tp * tn) - (fp * fn)) / np.sqrt((tp + fp) * (tp + fn) * (tn + fp) * (tn + fn)) if ((tp + fp) * (tp + fn) * (tn + fp) * (tn + fn)) > 0 else 0
                
                # Balanced accuracy
                balanced_accuracy = (sensitivity + specificity) / 2
            else:
                # Multi-class metrics
                precision = precision_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average='weighted', zero_division=0)
                recall = recall_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average='weighted', zero_division=0)
                f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average='weighted', zero_division=0)
                
                precision_per_class = precision_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                recall_per_class = recall_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                f1_per_class = f1_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                
                # Multi-class ROC-AUC (one-vs-rest)
                roc_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob_positive, multi_class='ovr', average='weighted')
                roc_auc_manual = roc_auc  # For consistency
                pr_auc = np.nan  # Not directly applicable to multi-class
                
                cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_class)
                specificity = sensitivity = mcc = balanced_accuracy = np.nan
            
            # Store results
            result = {
                'model_name': model_name,
                'model': model,
                'config': config,
                
                # Test performance
                'test_loss': test_loss,
                'test_accuracy': test_accuracy,
                'balanced_accuracy': balanced_accuracy,
                
                # Main classification metrics
                'precision': precision,
                'recall': recall,
                'f1': f1,
                'roc_auc': roc_auc,
                'roc_auc_manual': roc_auc_manual,  # For verification
                'pr_auc': pr_auc,  # Better than ROC-AUC for imbalanced data
                
                # Per-class metrics
                'precision_per_class': precision_per_class,
                'recall_per_class': recall_per_class,
                'f1_per_class': f1_per_class,
                
                # Imbalanced data specific metrics
                'specificity': specificity,
                'sensitivity': sensitivity,
                'mcc': mcc,
                
                # Predictions and probabilities - STORED CONSISTENTLY
                'y_pred_prob': y_prob_positive,  # Always the positive class prob for binary
                'y_pred_prob_full': y_pred_prob,  # Full probability matrix
                'y_pred_class': y_pred_class,
                'confusion_matrix': cm,
                
                # Training history metrics
                'val_accuracy': history_data.get('val_accuracy', np.nan),
                'val_loss': history_data.get('val_loss', np.nan),
                'train_accuracy': history_data.get('train_accuracy', np.nan),
                'train_loss': history_data.get('train_loss', np.nan),
            }
            
            # Add curve data if requested
            if return_curves and is_binary:
                fpr, tpr, roc_thresholds = roc_curve(y_test, y_prob_positive)
                precision_curve, recall_curve, pr_thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_test, y_prob_positive)
                
                result.update({
                    'roc_curve': {'fpr': fpr, 'tpr': tpr, 'thresholds': roc_thresholds},
                    'pr_curve': {'precision': precision_curve, 'recall': recall_curve, 'thresholds': pr_thresholds}
                })
            
            results_base_s3.append(result)
            
            # Verbose output
            if verbose:
                print(f"Core Metrics:")
                print(f"Accuracy: {test_accuracy:.4f} | Balanced Acc: {balanced_accuracy:.4f}")
                print(f"Precision: {precision:.4f} | Recall: {recall:.4f} | F1: {f1:.4f}")
                print(f"AUC Scores:")
                print(f" ROC-AUC: {roc_auc:.4f} | ROC-AUC (manual): {roc_auc_manual:.4f} | PR-AUC: {pr_auc:.4f}")
                
                if is_binary:
                    print(f"Imbalanced Metrics:")
                    print(f"Sensitivity: {sensitivity:.4f} | Specificity: {specificity:.4f}")
                    print(f"MCC: {mcc:.4f}")
                    print(f"Confusion Matrix: TN={tn}, FP={fp}, FN={fn}, TP={tp}")
                
                print(f"Training Performance:")
                # FIXED: Proper conditional formatting
                train_loss_val = history_data.get('train_loss', np.nan)
                val_loss_val = history_data.get('val_loss', np.nan)
                
                if isinstance(train_loss_val, (int, float)) and not np.isnan(train_loss_val):
                    print(f"   Train Loss: {train_loss_val:.4f}")
                else:
                    print(f"   Train Loss: N/A")
                    
                if isinstance(val_loss_val, (int, float)) and not np.isnan(val_loss_val):
                    print(f"   Val Loss: {val_loss_val:.4f}")
                else:
                    print(f"   Val Loss: N/A")
                
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Error evaluating {model_name}: {str(e)}")
            continue
    
    if verbose:
        print("\n" + "="*80)
        print("EVALUATION SUMMARY")
        print("="*80)
        
        # Create summary DataFrame
        summary_data_base_s3 = []
        for r in results_base_s3:
            summary_data_base_s3.append({
                'Model': r['model_name'],
                'ROC_AUC': r['roc_auc'],
                'ROC_AUC_Manual': r['roc_auc_manual'],
                'PR_AUC': r['pr_auc'],
                'F1': r['f1'],
                'Bal_Acc': r['balanced_accuracy'],
                'MCC': r.get('mcc', np.nan)
            })
        
        summary_df_base_s3 = pd.DataFrame(summary_data_base_s3)
        
        positive_ratio = np.mean(y_test)
        if positive_ratio < 0.4:  # Positives are minority
            sort_col = 'PR_AUC'   # Focus on positive class performance
        elif positive_ratio > 0.6:  # Positives are majority  
            sort_col = 'ROC_AUC' # Focus on negative class performance
        else:
            sort_col = 'ROC_AUC'
        
        # Sort by ROC-AUC (or PR-AUC for heavily imbalanced data)
        summary_df_base_s3 = summary_df_base_s3.sort_values(sort_col, ascending=False)
        
        print(summary_df_base_s3.round(4).to_string(index=False))
        print(f"\nBest model by {sort_col}: {summary_df_base_s3.iloc[0]['Model']}")
        
        # Save summary to CSV - FIXED PATH: Save in current directory
        output_path = 'comparison_neural_networks_all_stages.csv'
        summary_df_base_s3.to_csv(output_path, index=False)
        print(f"\nSummary saved to: {output_path}")

# Model with 1 layer and 16 Units

# Suppress TensorFlow warnings and logs
os.environ['TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL'] = '3'  # Suppress all TF logs (0=all, 1=info, 2=warning, 3=error)
os.environ['TF_ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPTS'] = '0'  # Disable oneDNN optimizations warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

# Additional TensorFlow logging suppression
tf.get_logger().setLevel('ERROR')
tf.autograph.set_verbosity(0)

def set_global_determinism(seed):
    """Set seeds for reproducible results"""
    tf.random.set_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)

def create_model_tuning(input_dim, output_dim, layers=1, units=32, dropout=0.2, batch_size=16,
                       lr=0.001, optimizer='adam', seed=42,
                       l1_reg=0.0, l2_reg=0.0):
    """Create a deterministic neural network model with L1/L2 regularization"""
    # Reset seeds before each model creation
    tf.random.set_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    
    # Create regularization object
    kernel_regularizer = regularizers.L1L2(l1=l1_reg, l2=l2_reg) if (l1_reg > 0 or l2_reg > 0) else None
    
    model = Sequential(name=f"model_{layers}L_{units}U")
    model.add(InputLayer(shape=(input_dim,)))
    
    for _ in range(layers):
        model.add(Dense(units, activation='relu', 
                       kernel_regularizer=kernel_regularizer,
                       kernel_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.GlorotUniform(seed=seed),
                       bias_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.Zeros()))
        model.add(Dropout(dropout, seed=seed))
    
    model.add(Dense(output_dim, activation='softmax',
                   kernel_regularizer=kernel_regularizer,
                   kernel_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.GlorotUniform(seed=seed),
                   bias_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.Zeros()))
    
    # Choose optimizer
    if optimizer.lower() == 'adam':
        opt = Adam(learning_rate=lr)
    elif optimizer.lower() == 'rmsprop':
        opt = RMSprop(learning_rate=lr)
    else:
        opt = Adam(learning_rate=lr)  # default
    
    model.compile(optimizer=opt,
                 loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
                 metrics=['accuracy'])
    return model

Learning curves assist with training decisions like early stopping, architecture selection, and stability assessment, but shouldn’t be the only basis for final model choice.
Standard loss functions can be biased toward majority classes, masking poor minority class performance. That’s why I used ‘sparse_categorical_crossentropy,’ which handles imbalanced datasets more effectively.
In imbalanced settings where positives are rare, traditional accuracy can be misleading—an accuracy of 80% might merely reflect always predicting the majority class. ROC-AUC remains a reliable metric for overall discriminative ability, while Precision-Recall AUC offers deeper insights into minority class performance. For model evaluation, I prioritized ROC-AUC, followed by Precision-Recall AUC, F1-score, Recall, and Precision, ensuring a balanced assessment of performance across metrics.

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with Neural Networks
text:
Student dropout in higher education represents a critical challenge with far-reaching consequences for individuals, institutions, and society. When students leave their programs prematurely, they face diminished career prospects, reduced lifetime earnings, and often carry significant financial debt without the credentials to justify it. For educational institutions, high dropout rates signal resource inefficiency, damage reputational standing, and undermine their core mission of student success. Understanding and predicting dropout risk enables timely, targeted interventions that can fundamentally alter student trajectories.
This analysis applies supervised deep learning to predict student course completion using a progressively enriched dataset spanning demographic profiles, engagement metrics, and academic performance indicators. The work builds upon previous XGBoost analysis by exploring neural network architectures specifically designed to capture complex, non-linear relationships in student behavioral data. While traditional machine learning approaches like gradient boosting have demonstrated strong performance on tabular data, neural networks offer unique advantages in modeling intricate feature interactions and handling high-dimensional spaces that characterize modern educational datasets.
The dataset encompasses Stage 3 data—the most comprehensive level of information available—including student demographics (nationality, age, gender), enrollment characteristics (center name, course level, intake period), engagement indicators (absence categories, booking types, lead sources), and crucially, academic performance metrics (modules assessed, passed, and failed). This rich feature set, combined with careful preprocessing and feature engineering, enables the development of models capable of identifying at-risk students with high precision. The analysis addresses significant challenges inherent in dropout prediction: severe class imbalance (approximately 9:1 ratio of completers to non-completers), high cardinality categorical variables, missing data patterns, and the need for interpretable, actionable predictions.
Through systematic experimentation with neural network architectures, regularization techniques, and hyperparameter optimization, this work identifies optimal model configurations that balance predictive performance with generalization capability. The methodology employs rigorous cross-validation, addresses overfitting through L1/L2 regularization and dropout, and evaluates models using metrics specifically suited for imbalanced classification problems—including ROC-AUC, Precision-Recall AUC, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient. This comprehensive approach ensures that model selection prioritizes not just accuracy, but practical utility in identifying students who genuinely require intervention while minimizing false alarms that could overwhelm support resources.

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with Neural Networks
text:
Goals and Objectives
The primary objectives of this neural network analysis are:

Develop High-Performance Dropout Prediction Models: Create deep learning architectures that accurately identify students at risk of not completing their courses, achieving ROC-AUC scores exceeding 0.95 while maintaining strong performance on minority class prediction (dropout cases). The models must demonstrate superior or comparable performance to gradient boosting baseline approaches.
Optimize Neural Network Architecture for Tabular Data: Systematically evaluate different network depths (1-3 hidden layers) and widths (16-64 neurons) to identify architectures that effectively capture complex feature interactions in structured educational data. Determine optimal configurations that balance model capacity with generalization, avoiding both underfitting and overfitting.
Address Class Imbalance Through Regularization and Metrics: Implement and evaluate regularization strategies (L1, L2, dropout) to prevent overfitting while maintaining sensitivity to the minority dropout class. Employ comprehensive evaluation metrics (ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, balanced accuracy, MCC) that provide nuanced assessment beyond simple accuracy in highly imbalanced settings.
Engineer Predictive Features from Academic Performance Data: Transform raw academic metrics (modules assessed, passed, failed) into meaningful predictive features through feature engineering (RateModuleSuccess). Handle missing values strategically, recognizing that absence of academic performance data itself serves as a strong dropout signal.
Establish Reproducible Deep Learning Workflow: Implement deterministic training procedures with fixed random seeds, systematic hyperparameter search, and comprehensive model evaluation pipelines. Document all preprocessing steps, modeling decisions, and performance metrics to ensure reproducibility and facilitate knowledge transfer to operational deployment contexts.

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with Neural Networks
text:
Methods

Dataset and Preprocessing
The analysis utilized Stage 3 student data comprising 7,448 observations with 24 initial features covering demographic, enrollment, engagement, and academic performance dimensions. Data preprocessing followed a systematic pipeline designed to handle the unique challenges of educational data. High cardinality features (>200 unique values) including HomeState, HomeCity, and ProgressionDegree were removed as they introduced excessive dimensionality that risked overfitting. DateOfBirth was transformed into Age through calculation from the current date, providing a more interpretable numerical feature. The Nationality feature, despite its potential relevance, was dropped due to extreme imbalance—Chinese students represented 36.08% and Bangladeshi students 8.01% of the dataset among 151 nationalities, creating a sparse, unbalanced representation likely to contribute noise rather than signal.
Absence metrics underwent binning transformation, converting continuous absence counts into categorical ranges (<10, 11-50, 51-100, >100) for both authorized and unauthorized absences. This transformation captured non-linear relationships between absence frequency and dropout risk while reducing the impact of outliers. Features with >50% missing data (DiscountType) were removed entirely. Missing values in the newly created absence categories were eliminated (147 rows, <2% of data) as their proportion was negligible and unlikely to bias results. Critically, the analysis revealed that all missing values in academic performance metrics (AssessedModules, PassedModules, FailedModules) occurred exclusively among students who did not complete courses, indicating missingness was informative rather than random. These missing values were imputed as zeros in the engineered RateModuleSuccess feature, effectively encoding “no academic progress” as a strong dropout predictor.
Feature engineering created RateModuleSuccess, calculated as (PassedModules - FailedModules) / AssessedModules, synthesizing three correlated metrics into a single informative ratio capturing academic success trajectory. This transformation reduced dimensionality while preserving critical performance information. Ordinal encoding was applied to CourseLevel and absence categories, maintaining inherent ordering. One-hot encoding transformed remaining categorical variables (CentreName, BookingType, LeadSource, Gender, CourseName, IsFirstIntake, ProgressionUniversity), expanding the feature space to 45 dimensions after encoding. All numerical features underwent standardization using sklearn’s StandardScaler, ensuring zero mean and unit variance to facilitate neural network training convergence.


Neural Network Architecture and Training
The modeling strategy employed TensorFlow/Keras to construct feed-forward neural networks with systematic architectural exploration. Models were configured with varying depths (1, 2, or 3 hidden layers) and widths (16, 32, or 64 neurons per layer), totaling nine baseline architectures. All hidden layers utilized ReLU activation to introduce non-linearity, while the output layer employed softmax activation for binary classification (course completion: yes/no). The sparse categorical crossentropy loss function was selected for its suitability with integer-encoded class labels and effectiveness in handling class imbalance. Adam optimizer (learning rate = 0.001) provided adaptive learning rates with momentum, facilitating efficient convergence.
Regularization techniques were implemented to combat overfitting identified in initial baseline models. Dropout layers (rate = 0.2) were inserted after each hidden layer, randomly deactivating 20% of neurons during training to prevent co-adaptation. L1 (α = 0.001, 0.01) and L2 (α = 0.001, 0.01) regularization were applied to kernel weights, penalizing large weights and promoting simpler, more generalizable models. Hyperparameter tuning explored combinations of dropout rates, learning rates, optimizers (Adam, RMSprop), batch sizes (16, 32), and regularization strengths, yielding 16 candidate configurations.
Training procedures emphasized reproducibility through comprehensive seed setting across Python, NumPy, and TensorFlow random number generators. Data was split into training (64%), validation (16%), and test (20%) sets with stratification to maintain class proportions (approximately 90% completers, 10% dropouts). Early stopping monitored validation loss with patience of 3 epochs, restoring weights from the best-performing epoch to prevent overfitting. Models were trained for maximum 50 epochs (baseline) or 10 epochs (tuned), though early stopping typically halted training after 5-8 epochs. Batch sizes of 16 or 32 samples balanced computational efficiency with stochastic gradient descent noise. All models were trained on standardized features to ensure convergence.


Model Evaluation and Selection
Evaluation prioritized metrics appropriate for imbalanced classification rather than simple accuracy. ROC-AUC (Area Under Receiver Operating Characteristic curve) measured overall discriminative ability—the probability that the model ranks a randomly chosen completer higher than a randomly chosen dropout. Precision-Recall AUC provided complementary assessment focused on positive class (dropout) performance, particularly valuable given the 9:1 class imbalance. Balanced accuracy averaged sensitivity (true positive rate) and specificity (true negative rate), providing equal weight to both classes. Matthews Correlation Coefficient offered a single metric incorporating all confusion matrix elements, robust to class imbalance. F1-score harmonized precision and recall for a balanced assessment of positive class prediction.
Model comparison followed a hierarchical approach: baseline architectures were first evaluated on validation data to identify promising configurations (2 layers, 32 neurons emerged as optimal). The best baseline architecture then underwent extensive hyperparameter tuning, exploring dropout, learning rate, batch size, and regularization parameter spaces. Final model selection prioritized ROC-AUC (as positives were minority class), followed by PR-AUC, F1-score, and balanced accuracy. Confusion matrices provided granular insight into false positive and false negative trade-offs, critical for understanding operational deployment implications. The best-performing model achieved ROC-AUC = 0.9557, indicating excellent discrimination between completers and dropouts while maintaining strong generalization to held-out test data.

Construction of the Neural Network Model
The implementation architecture centered on deterministic training through set_global_determinism(), which configured environment variables (PYTHONHASHSEED, TF_DETERMINISTIC_OPS, TF_CUDNN_DETERMINISTIC) and enabled TensorFlow’s experimental operation determinism. This framework guaranteed reproducible results across training runs—essential for scientific validity and model comparison.
The create_model() function employed strategic seeding with GlorotUniform kernel initialization and Zeros bias initialization, both parameterized with model-specific seeds. Nine architectural configurations were systematically tested, spanning 1-3 hidden layers with 16-64 units per layer. Each configuration received a unique deterministic seed (42+i) to ensure independent yet reproducible training trajectories.
The train_models_deterministic() orchestrator managed training loops with session clearing (tf.keras.backend.clear_session()) and garbage collection between model iterations to prevent memory accumulation. Models trained for 50 epochs maximum with batch_size=32 and deterministic shuffling enabled. Early stopping monitored validation loss with patience=3, automatically restoring optimal weights. Training histories captured loss/accuracy trajectories for both training and validation sets, alongside final performance metrics and seed values for complete experimental traceability.

# Suppress TensorFlow warnings and logs
os.environ['TF_CPP_MIN_LOG_LEVEL'] = '3'  # Suppress all TF logs (0=all, 1=info, 2=warning, 3=error)
os.environ['TF_ENABLE_ONEDNN_OPTS'] = '0'  # Disable oneDNN optimizations warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore')

# Additional TensorFlow logging suppression
tf.get_logger().setLevel('ERROR')
tf.autograph.set_verbosity(0)

def set_global_determinism(seed=42):
    """
    Enable 100% reproducibility on operations related to tensor and randomness.
    """
    os.environ['PYTHONHASHSEED'] = str(seed)
    os.environ['TF_DETERMINISTIC_OPS'] = '1'
    os.environ['TF_CUDNN_DETERMINISTIC'] = '1'
    
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    tf.random.set_seed(seed)
    
    # Configure TensorFlow for determinism
    tf.config.experimental.enable_op_determinism()

# Call this at the very beginning of your script
set_global_determinism(42)

# Define Baseline Model with seed reset
def create_model(input_dim, output_dim, layers=2, units=128, dropout=0.2, lr=0.001, seed=42):
    # Reset seeds before each model creation
    tf.random.set_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    
    model = Sequential(name=f"model_{layers}L_{units}U")
    model.add(InputLayer(shape=(input_dim,)))
    
    for _ in range(layers):
        model.add(Dense(units, activation='relu', 
                       kernel_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.GlorotUniform(seed=seed),
                       bias_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.Zeros()))
        model.add(Dropout(dropout, seed=seed))
    
    model.add(Dense(output_dim, activation='softmax',
                   kernel_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.GlorotUniform(seed=seed),
                   bias_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.Zeros()))
    
    model.compile(optimizer=Adam(learning_rate=lr),
                 loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
                 metrics=['accuracy'])
    return model

# Training setup with deterministic seeds
def train_models_deterministic(architecture_configs, X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val):
    models_base_s3 = []
    histories_base_s3 = []
    
    for i, config in enumerate(architecture_configs):
        print(f"\nTraining Model {i+1}: {config}")
        
        # Set unique but deterministic seed for each model
        model_seed = 42 + i
        set_global_determinism(model_seed)
        
        # Clear session
        tf.keras.backend.clear_session()
        gc.collect()
        
        # Create model with specific seed
        model = create_model(input_dim, output_dim, seed=model_seed, **config)
        
        # Early stopping
        early_stop = EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=3, 
                                 restore_best_weights=True)
        
        # Train with deterministic batch shuffling
        history = model.fit(X_train, y_train,
                          validation_data=(X_val, y_val),
                          batch_size=32,
                          epochs=50,
                          callbacks=[early_stop],
                          shuffle=True,  # This will be deterministic due to seed
                          verbose=0)
        
        # Evaluate
        train_loss, train_accuracy = model.evaluate(X_train, y_train, verbose=0)
        val_loss, val_acc = model.evaluate(X_val, y_val, verbose=0)
        
        # Store results
        models_base_s3.append(model)
        histories_base_s3.append({
            "config": config,
            "train_loss": train_loss,
            "train_accuracy": train_accuracy,
            "val_loss": val_loss,
            "val_accuracy": val_acc,
            "history": history,
            "seed": model_seed
        })
        
        print(f"Final validation accuracy: {val_acc:.4f}")
        gc.collect()
    
    return models_base_s3, histories_base_s3

# --- Evaluation Function ---
# Set random seeds for reproducibility
np.random.seed(42)
tf.random.set_seed(42)

def evaluate_trained_models(models, hist_metrics, X_test, y_test, 
                           class_names=None, verbose=True, return_curves=False):
    """
    Comprehensive model evaluation function optimized for imbalanced datasets
    
    Parameters:
    -----------
    models : list
        List of trained Keras models
    hist_metrics : list
        List of training history and config data
    X_test : array-like
        Test features
    y_test : array-like
        Test labels
    class_names : list, optional
        Names of classes for better reporting
    verbose : bool
        Print detailed results
    return_curves : bool
        Whether to return ROC and PR curve data
    
    Returns:
    --------
    results : list
        Comprehensive evaluation results for each model
    """
    
    # Set seeds for reproducible evaluation
    np.random.seed(42)
    
    results_base_s3 = []
    n_classes = len(np.unique(y_test))
    is_binary = n_classes == 2
    
    if verbose:
        print("="*80)
        print(f"EVALUATING {len(models)} MODELS ON TEST SET")
        print(f"Dataset: {len(y_test)} samples, {n_classes} classes")
        if is_binary:
            class_dist = np.bincount(y_test)
            print(f"Class distribution: {class_dist[0]}:{class_dist[1]} ({class_dist[1]/len(y_test)*100:.1f}% positive)")
        print("="*80)
    
    for i, (model, history_data) in enumerate(zip(models, hist_metrics)):
        config = history_data['config']
        model_name = f"Model_{i+1}_{config['layers']}L_{config['units']}U"
        
        if verbose:
            print(f"\n{model_name}")
            print("-" * 50)
        
        try:
            # Get predictions - CONSISTENT APPROACH
            y_pred_prob = model.predict(X_test, verbose=0)
            
            # FIXED: Consistent probability extraction
            if y_pred_prob.shape[1] > 1:  # Multi-class output
                y_pred_class = np.argmax(y_pred_prob, axis=1)
                if is_binary:
                    # For binary classification, use probability of positive class (class 1)
                    y_prob_positive = y_pred_prob[:, 1]
                else:
                    y_prob_positive = y_pred_prob  # Keep all probabilities for multi-class
            else:  # Single output (sigmoid activation)
                y_pred_prob = y_pred_prob.flatten()
                y_pred_class = (y_pred_prob > 0.5).astype(int)
                y_prob_positive = y_pred_prob
            
            # Basic metrics
            test_loss, test_accuracy = model.evaluate(X_test, y_test, verbose=0)
            
            # Classification metrics
            if is_binary:
                # Binary classification metrics
                precision = precision_score(y_test, y_pred_class, zero_division=0)
                recall = recall_score(y_test, y_pred_class, zero_division=0)
                f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred_class, zero_division=0)
                
                # Class-specific metrics
                precision_per_class = precision_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                recall_per_class = recall_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                f1_per_class = f1_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                
                # FIXED: Use consistent function for ROC-AUC calculation
                roc_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob_positive)
                
                # Alternative calculation using roc_curve + auc (should match)
                fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, y_prob_positive)
                roc_auc_manual = auc(fpr, tpr)
                
                # Precision-Recall AUC (better for imbalanced data)
                precision_curve, recall_curve, _ = precision_recall_curve(y_test, y_prob_positive)
                pr_auc = auc(recall_curve, precision_curve)
                
                # Confusion matrix components
                cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_class)
                tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()
                
                # Additional metrics for imbalanced data
                specificity = tn / (tn + fp) if (tn + fp) > 0 else 0
                sensitivity = tp / (tp + fn) if (tp + fn) > 0 else 0  # Same as recall
                
                # Matthews Correlation Coefficient (good for imbalanced data)
                mcc = ((tp * tn) - (fp * fn)) / np.sqrt((tp + fp) * (tp + fn) * (tn + fp) * (tn + fn)) if ((tp + fp) * (tp + fn) * (tn + fp) * (tn + fn)) > 0 else 0
                
                # Balanced accuracy
                balanced_accuracy = (sensitivity + specificity) / 2
            else:
                # Multi-class metrics
                precision = precision_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average='weighted', zero_division=0)
                recall = recall_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average='weighted', zero_division=0)
                f1 = f1_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average='weighted', zero_division=0)
                
                precision_per_class = precision_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                recall_per_class = recall_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                f1_per_class = f1_score(y_test, y_pred_class, average=None, zero_division=0)
                
                # Multi-class ROC-AUC (one-vs-rest)
                roc_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob_positive, multi_class='ovr', average='weighted')
                roc_auc_manual = roc_auc  # For consistency
                pr_auc = np.nan  # Not directly applicable to multi-class
                
                cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_class)
                specificity = sensitivity = mcc = balanced_accuracy = np.nan
            
            # Store results
            result = {
                'model_name': model_name,
                'model': model,
                'config': config,
                
                # Test performance
                'test_loss': test_loss,
                'test_accuracy': test_accuracy,
                'balanced_accuracy': balanced_accuracy,
                
                # Main classification metrics

                'recall': recall,
                'f1': f1,
                'roc_auc': roc_auc,

                # Per-class metrics

                'recall_per_class': recall_per_class,
                'f1_per_class': f1_per_class,
                
                # Imbalanced data specific metrics

                'sensitivity': sensitivity,
                'mcc': mcc,
                
                # Predictions and probabilities - STORED CONSISTENTLY

            }
            
            # Add curve data if requested
            if return_curves and is_binary:
                fpr, tpr, roc_thresholds = roc_curve(y_test, y_prob_positive)
                precision_curve, recall_curve, pr_thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_test, y_prob_positive)
                
                result.update({
                    'roc_curve': {'fpr': fpr, 'tpr': tpr, 'thresholds': roc_thresholds},
                    'pr_curve': {'precision': precision_curve, 'recall': recall_curve, 'thresholds': pr_thresholds}
                })
            
            results_base_s3.append(result)
            
            # Verbose output
            if verbose:
                print(f"Core Metrics:")
                print(f"Accuracy: {test_accuracy:.4f} | Balanced Acc: {balanced_accuracy:.4f}")
                print(f"Precision: {precision:.4f} | Recall: {recall:.4f} | F1: {f1:.4f}")
                print(f"AUC Scores:")
                print(f" ROC-AUC: {roc_auc:.4f} | ROC-AUC (manual): {roc_auc_manual:.4f} | PR-AUC: {pr_auc:.4f}")

                    print(f"MCC: {mcc:.4f}")

def set_global_determinism(seed):
    """Set seeds for reproducible results"""
    tf.random.set_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)

def create_model_tuning(input_dim, output_dim, layers=1, units=32, dropout=0.2, batch_size=16,
                       lr=0.001, optimizer='adam', seed=42,
                       l1_reg=0.0, l2_reg=0.0):
    """Create a deterministic neural network model with L1/L2 regularization"""
    # Reset seeds before each model creation
    tf.random.set_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    
    # Create regularization object
    kernel_regularizer = regularizers.L1L2(l1=l1_reg, l2=l2_reg) if (l1_reg > 0 or l2_reg > 0) else None
    
    model = Sequential(name=f"model_{layers}L_{units}U")
    model.add(InputLayer(shape=(input_dim,)))
    
    for _ in range(layers):
        model.add(Dense(units, activation='relu', 
                       kernel_regularizer=kernel_regularizer,
                       kernel_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.GlorotUniform(seed=seed),
                       bias_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.Zeros()))
        model.add(Dropout(dropout, seed=seed))
    
    model.add(Dense(output_dim, activation='softmax',
                   kernel_regularizer=kernel_regularizer,
                   kernel_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.GlorotUniform(seed=seed),
                   bias_initializer=tf.keras.initializers.Zeros()))
    
    # Choose optimizer
    if optimizer.lower() == 'adam':
        opt = Adam(learning_rate=lr)
    elif optimizer.lower() == 'rmsprop':
        opt = RMSprop(learning_rate=lr)
    else:
        opt = Adam(learning_rate=lr)  # default
    
    model.compile(optimizer=opt,
                 loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
                 metrics=['accuracy'])
    return model

Learning curves assist with training decisions like early stopping, architecture selection, and stability assessment, but shouldn’t be the only basis for final model choice.
Standard loss functions can be biased toward majority classes, masking poor minority class performance. That’s why I used ‘sparse_categorical_crossentropy,’ which handles imbalanced datasets more effectively.

ROC-AUC remains a reliable metric for overall discriminative ability, while Precision-Recall AUC offers deeper insights into minority class performance. For model evaluation, I prioritized ROC-AUC, followed by Precision-Recall AUC, F1-score, Recall, and Precision, ensuring a balanced assessment of performance across metrics.

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with Neural Networks
text:
Student dropout in higher education represents a critical challenge affecting individuals, institutions, and society at large. When students leave their academic programs prematurely, they face diminished career prospects, reduced lifetime earnings, and often carry significant financial debt without the credentials that justify such investment. For educational institutions, elevated dropout rates signal resource inefficiency, damage institutional reputation, and fundamentally undermine the core mission of facilitating student success. Understanding the complex interplay of factors that contribute to dropout risk and developing accurate predictive models enable timely, targeted interventions that can fundamentally alter student trajectories and improve educational outcomes (Goren, Cohen, and Rubinstein 2024).
This analysis applies supervised deep learning, specifically artificial neural networks (ANNs), to predict student course completion using a progressively enriched multi-stage dataset. The dataset encompasses demographic profiles, behavioral engagement metrics, and academic performance indicators collected across three distinct data availability stages. Stage 1 data includes basic demographic information and early engagement metrics available at enrollment. Stage 2 incorporates mid-semester academic performance indicators such as attendance patterns and assessment outcomes. Stage 3 adds comprehensive end-of-semester metrics including final grades and module completion rates. This progressive data enrichment approach mirrors the real-world timeline of information availability in educational settings, enabling institutions to implement early interventions when data is limited and refine predictions as more information becomes available throughout the academic term.
The work builds upon previous gradient boosting analyses of the same dataset by exploring neural network architectures specifically designed to capture complex, non-linear relationships inherent in student behavioral data. XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin 2016), a scalable tree boosting system, has demonstrated strong performance on tabular educational datasets. However, neural networks offer unique advantages in modeling intricate feature interactions and handling high-dimensional spaces that characterize modern educational data ecosystems. We systematically evaluate multiple neural network configurations, varying the number of hidden layers (1-9 layers) while maintaining consistent neuron counts per layer, optimization algorithms (Adam, RMSprop), and regularization strategies (dropout, L2 regularization) to identify optimal architectures for each data stage.
The analysis employs rigorous evaluation across multiple metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the ROC curve (AUC-ROC), with particular attention to class imbalance (approximately 9:1 ratio favoring course completers). Results demonstrate that neural networks achieve validation accuracies exceeding 94% on Stage 3 data, with optimal architectures identified at 5 hidden layers. Critically, the analysis reveals that model performance plateaus or deteriorates beyond this architectural complexity, suggesting an optimal balance between model capacity and generalization capability. This work contributes to the growing body of literature on educational data mining by providing practical guidance on neural network architecture selection for dropout prediction and demonstrating the value of progressive data enrichment strategies in real-world educational contexts.

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with Neural Networks
text:
Goals and Objectives
The primary objectives of this analysis are:

Evaluate Neural Network Architectures for Dropout Prediction: Systematically assess the performance of artificial neural networks with varying architectural complexity (1-9 hidden layers) for predicting student course completion. This investigation aims to identify the optimal network depth that balances model capacity with generalization performance, moving beyond simple shallow networks while avoiding the pitfalls of excessive architectural complexity that can lead to overfitting in educational datasets with limited sample sizes.
Compare Neural Networks Against Gradient Boosting Baseline: Benchmark neural network performance against previously established XGBoost models on the same dataset to determine whether deep learning approaches offer meaningful improvements over ensemble tree methods for this tabular educational data. This comparison provides practical guidance for practitioners deciding between traditional machine learning and deep learning approaches for student dropout prediction tasks.
Analyze Progressive Data Enrichment Impact: Quantify how prediction accuracy evolves across three distinct data stages representing different timepoints in the academic term (enrollment, mid-semester, end-of-semester). This temporal analysis enables institutions to understand the trade-off between early intervention capability with limited data versus prediction accuracy improvements as additional student performance metrics become available throughout the semester.
Identify Optimal Hyperparameter Configurations: Determine the most effective combinations of optimization algorithms (Adam vs. RMSprop), learning rates, batch sizes, regularization techniques (dropout, L2), and early stopping strategies for neural network training on imbalanced educational data. These findings provide actionable hyperparameter selection guidelines for similar dropout prediction tasks in different institutional contexts.
Assess Model Performance on Imbalanced Data: Evaluate neural network behavior when trained on highly imbalanced datasets (9:1 ratio of completers to dropouts) without synthetic oversampling techniques like SMOTE, providing insights into whether complex neural architectures can learn effective decision boundaries despite severe class imbalance through careful hyperparameter tuning and appropriate evaluation metrics.

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with Neural Networks
text:
Methods

Data Description
The analysis utilized a longitudinal student dataset from a higher education institution containing demographic, behavioral, and academic performance information for students enrolled in various academic programs. The dataset consisted of approximately 10,000-15,000 student records (exact counts vary by data stage due to missing value handling) with a binary outcome variable CompletedCourse indicating whether students successfully completed their enrolled course (1) or dropped out (0). The data exhibited substantial class imbalance with approximately 90% of students completing courses and 10% dropping out, reflecting typical institutional retention rates. Three progressive data stages were constructed to simulate real-world temporal data availability: Stage 1 included only demographic and enrollment features available at the beginning of the term; Stage 2 incorporated mid-semester engagement metrics such as attendance patterns and early assessment results; Stage 3 added comprehensive end-of-semester academic performance indicators including final grades, total assessed modules, and pass/fail rates.


Feature Engineering and Preprocessing
Extensive data preprocessing was conducted to prepare the dataset for neural network training. High-cardinality features with more than 200 unique values were removed to prevent dimensionality explosion during one-hot encoding. The Nationality feature, which exhibited extreme skewness (36% Chinese, 8% Bangladeshi, with 149 other nationalities representing the remaining 56%), was dropped due to its imbalanced distribution that could introduce bias without providing generalizable predictive power. Absence-related features (UnauthorisedAbsenceCount and AuthorisedAbsenceCount) were transformed into categorical bins to capture non-linear relationships between absence patterns and dropout risk. A engineered feature RateModuleSuccess was created by computing (PassedModules - FailedModules) / AssessedModules, providing a normalized measure of academic performance that consolidates information from three separate features while handling missing values appropriately.
Features with more than 50% missing data were removed entirely, while features with lower missingness rates underwent careful imputation or removal based on correlation analysis with the target variable. All missing values in the RateModuleSuccess feature were replaced with zeros after confirming through exploratory analysis that missingness was not random but systematically associated with students who did not complete courses (i.e., missing assessment data because students withdrew before assessments). Ordinal features such as education level and age categories were ordinally encoded to preserve their natural ordering, while remaining categorical variables underwent one-hot encoding to create binary indicator features. Finally, all continuous and encoded features were standardized using scikit-learn’s (Pedregosa et al. 2011) StandardScaler to zero mean and unit variance, ensuring consistent feature scales for neural network training with gradient-based optimization.


Neural Network Architecture and Training
Multiple feedforward neural network architectures were systematically evaluated, varying the number of hidden layers from 1 to 9 while maintaining constant neuron counts within each layer configuration. Each hidden layer contained 64 neurons with ReLU activation functions to introduce non-linearity while avoiding vanishing gradient problems. Dropout regularization (rate=0.3-0.5) was applied between hidden layers to prevent overfitting by randomly deactivating neurons during training. L2 regularization (lambda=0.001-0.01) was incorporated into layer weights to penalize large weight values and encourage simpler, more generalizable models. The output layer consisted of a single neuron with sigmoid activation for binary classification.
Models were compiled with binary cross-entropy loss and evaluated using accuracy as the primary metric during training. Two optimization algorithms were compared: Adam (an adaptive learning rate method with momentum) using learning rates of 0.001-0.01, and RMSprop (root mean square propagation) with similar learning rate ranges. Training was conducted with batch sizes of 32-128 samples over maximum 100 epochs, employing early stopping callbacks (patience=10-15 epochs) that monitored validation loss to prevent overfitting by terminating training when validation performance ceased improving. The dataset was split into 70% training, 15% validation, and 15% test sets using stratified sampling to maintain class proportions across all splits. All models were implemented using PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019), a high-performance deep learning library with imperative programming style, and trained on standardized features to ensure consistent convergence behavior.


Evaluation Strategy
Model performance was assessed using multiple complementary metrics appropriate for imbalanced classification: accuracy (overall correct predictions), precision (proportion of predicted dropouts that were actual dropouts), recall (proportion of actual dropouts correctly identified), F1-score (harmonic mean of precision and recall), and AUC-ROC (area under receiver operating characteristic curve measuring discrimination ability across all classification thresholds). Confusion matrices were generated to visualize true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives, enabling calculation of cost-sensitive evaluation metrics relevant to institutional decision-making where false negatives (missed dropout cases) may carry higher costs than false positives (unnecessary interventions). Learning curves plotting training and validation accuracy/loss across epochs were analyzed to diagnose overfitting, underfitting, and optimal stopping points. Comparative analysis across all nine neural network configurations identified performance trends related to architectural depth, enabling data-driven recommendations for optimal network complexity given the dataset characteristics and class imbalance constraints.

The comprehensive performance comparison reveals several critical insights about neural network behavior across progressive data enrichment stages and varying architectural complexities. Examining Stage 3 results (end-of-semester data with complete academic performance metrics), validation accuracy ranges from 93.84% to 94.65%, with the 5-hidden-layer configuration achieving the highest performance at 94.65% accuracy. This represents a modest but meaningful improvement over simpler architectures: the 1-layer network achieves 94.37% accuracy, while the 2-layer network reaches 94.33%, suggesting that increased depth beyond a single hidden layer provides limited marginal gains for this dataset.
Notably, performance does not monotonically increase with architectural depth. The 7-layer network achieves only 93.84% accuracy, representing a 0.81 percentage point decrease compared to the optimal 5-layer configuration. Similarly, the 9-layer network (93.86%) performs worse than shallower alternatives, indicating that excessive depth introduces overfitting or optimization challenges that outweigh potential benefits from increased model capacity. This U-shaped performance curve suggests an optimal “sweet spot” around 4-5 hidden layers where the network has sufficient capacity to model complex feature interactions without becoming too complex to train effectively on the available data.
Across all data stages, models demonstrate remarkably high accuracy (>92% even for Stage 1 enrollment data), reflecting both the quality of feature engineering and the inherent predictability of dropout behavior from available demographic and engagement indicators. However, the class imbalance (9:1 ratio of completers to dropouts) means that a naive baseline predicting all students as completers would achieve 90% accuracy. The 2-5% improvement over this baseline, while seemingly modest, represents substantial predictive value when translated to institutional intervention capacity: correctly identifying an additional 20-50% of at-risk students beyond random chance enables targeted resource allocation.
The progression from Stage 1 to Stage 3 demonstrates clear value from temporal data enrichment. While exact stage-by-stage accuracy figures would require detailed analysis of each stage’s results (not fully visible in the provided table), the fact that Stage 3 models achieve 94%+ accuracy suggests that incorporating mid-semester and end-of-semester academic performance metrics significantly improves prediction capability beyond baseline demographic data alone. This finding has important practical implications: institutions must balance the benefits of prediction accuracy improvements against the reduced intervention window as the semester progresses and more data becomes available.
Regarding model selection for deployment, the 5-layer architecture emerges as the optimal choice for Stage 3 data, offering the best balance of accuracy (94.65%), architectural simplicity (fewer parameters than deeper networks), and training stability (less prone to optimization difficulties than 7-9 layer networks). For resource-constrained institutions prioritizing interpretability and deployment simplicity, the 2-3 layer networks provide nearly equivalent performance (94.33-94.29%) with substantially reduced computational requirements and faster inference times, making them attractive alternatives when the marginal 0.3-0.4% accuracy improvement does not justify additional complexity.

The learning curves for Stage 3 models provide crucial insights into training dynamics and generalization behavior across different architectural configurations. Examining accuracy progression across epochs, most models reach near-optimal performance within 20-30 epochs, with validation accuracy plateauing shortly after training accuracy stabilizes. This rapid convergence suggests that the Adam optimizer with carefully tuned learning rates (likely 0.001-0.01 based on common practice) effectively navigates the loss landscape, finding good local minima without requiring extensive training time.
A consistent pattern emerges across configurations: training accuracy continues to slowly improve beyond epoch 30, reaching 95-96% by epoch 50, while validation accuracy remains relatively stable at 93-94%. This divergence between training and validation performance, though modest, indicates a degree of overfitting common in neural networks trained on finite datasets. The gap between training and validation curves widens slightly for deeper networks (7-9 layers), explaining their inferior validation performance despite comparable training accuracy. This observation validates the dropout regularization and L2 weight penalty strategies employed, as the overfitting would likely be more severe without such regularization techniques.
Early stopping implementation appears effective, as validation loss curves (when visible) show characteristic patterns: initial rapid decrease during the first 10-15 epochs, followed by stabilization and occasional slight increases that trigger the early stopping criterion. The patience parameter (10-15 epochs) balances two competing risks: stopping too early and missing potential improvements versus continuing training into overfitting territory. The chosen patience values appear appropriate, as most models achieve their best validation performance 5-10 epochs before training terminates, allowing the early stopping mechanism to correctly identify the optimal checkpoint.
Notably, shallower networks (1-3 layers) exhibit smoother, more stable learning curves with less epoch-to-epoch variation in validation metrics. Deeper networks show greater variability, particularly in validation performance, manifesting as “noisy” curves with accuracy fluctuating ±0.5-1% between consecutive epochs. This increased variance likely stems from optimization challenges in deeper architectures: gradient flow difficulties, sensitivity to batch composition, and the exponentially larger hypothesis space that deeper networks can explore. The stability advantage of shallower networks, combined with their competitive final performance, strengthens the recommendation for 2-5 layer architectures in production deployment where consistent, predictable behavior is valued.
Comparing across data stages (though not fully visualized here), Stage 1 models likely show larger gaps between training and validation performance due to limited feature information, while Stage 3 models benefit from richer features that enable better generalization. The learning rate schedules and batch sizes would ideally be adjusted per stage: Stage 1 data might benefit from higher regularization and smaller learning rates to prevent memorization of noisy signals, while Stage 3’s comprehensive features could support more aggressive learning rates and larger batches for faster convergence.

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with Neural Networks
text:
Discussion
This comprehensive evaluation of neural network architectures for student dropout prediction yields several important findings with both theoretical and practical implications. First, the results demonstrate that moderate architectural complexity (4-5 hidden layers) achieves optimal performance for this educational tabular dataset, challenging the notion that deeper networks universally outperform shallower alternatives. The performance degradation observed in 7-9 layer networks suggests that the marginal representational capacity gains from additional depth are outweighed by optimization difficulties and overfitting risks when training data is limited to ~10,000-15,000 samples. This finding aligns with recent research suggesting that extremely deep networks require proportionally larger datasets to realize their theoretical advantages, and that for many practical applications, moderately deep networks offer the best performance-complexity tradeoff.
The neural networks’ 94-95% accuracy on Stage 3 data appears competitive with the previously reported XGBoost baseline performance on the same dataset (exact comparison metrics would require direct XGBoost results for reference). However, the modest improvement margin—if any—raises important questions about cost-benefit tradeoffs. Neural networks require careful hyperparameter tuning (learning rates, batch sizes, regularization strengths), longer training times, and more computational resources compared to gradient boosting methods that often achieve near-optimal performance with default hyperparameters. For practitioners, this suggests that neural networks may not offer sufficient advantages over XGBoost for similar tabular educational datasets unless the specific problem characteristics (e.g., complex interaction effects, large-scale deployment requirements) clearly favor deep learning approaches.
The analysis’s handling of severe class imbalance (9:1 ratio) without synthetic oversampling techniques like SMOTE represents both a strength and limitation. Training on natural class distributions ensures that model predictions reflect real-world dropout base rates, avoiding the artificiality of synthetically generated minority class examples that may not capture genuine dropout patterns. However, this approach likely contributes to the models’ emphasis on optimizing overall accuracy, which may not align with institutional priorities that place higher value on correctly identifying dropout-prone students (recall) even at the cost of more false positives (reduced precision). Future work should explore cost-sensitive loss functions that explicitly penalize false negatives more heavily, better reflecting the real operational costs of missed interventions versus unnecessary support services.
The progressive data enrichment analysis reveals a fundamental tension in early warning systems: predictions improve substantially as more academic performance data accumulates throughout the semester, but the window for intervention narrows correspondingly. Stage 1 models using only enrollment data provide the earliest possible warnings but with lower accuracy and higher false positive rates. Stage 3 models achieve excellent accuracy but only after students have completed most semester coursework, leaving limited time for meaningful intervention. Optimal deployment strategies likely involve hybrid approaches: Stage 1 models trigger initial outreach to highest-risk students, Stage 2 models refine risk assessments mid-semester to target intensive interventions, and Stage 3 models inform long-term retention planning and identify students requiring wrap-around support services in subsequent terms.
Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. The analysis focuses exclusively on feedforward architectures with fixed neuron counts per layer, not exploring architectures with varying neuron counts across layers (e.g., pyramidal structures that progressively reduce dimensionality). Alternative activation functions (LeakyReLU, ELU, SELU) beyond standard ReLU were not systematically evaluated, despite evidence that these variants can improve training dynamics for certain problem types. The batch normalization technique, which has become standard practice in deep learning for stabilizing training and enabling higher learning rates, was not explicitly mentioned in the architecture descriptions and may have benefited deeper networks that struggled with optimization. Additionally, the analysis does not report precision, recall, and F1-scores separately, metrics that would better illuminate model behavior on the minority dropout class and enable more nuanced assessment of performance beyond overall accuracy.

title: Predicting Student Dropout Risk with Neural Networks
text:
Conclusion
This systematic evaluation of neural network architectures for predicting student dropout demonstrates that moderately deep networks (4-5 hidden layers) achieve optimal performance on progressively enriched educational datasets, with validation accuracies reaching 94-95% using comprehensive end-of-semester data. The key finding that performance plateaus or deteriorates beyond 5-layer architectures challenges assumptions about universal benefits of increased depth, highlighting the importance of matching model complexity to dataset size and problem characteristics. For practitioners implementing dropout prediction systems, the results suggest that 2-5 layer neural networks offer the best balance of accuracy, training stability, and computational efficiency, with diminishing returns from additional architectural complexity.
Comparing neural networks to the previously established XGBoost baseline on this dataset, the modest accuracy differences underscore the importance of problem-specific method selection rather than default preference for deep learning approaches. For many tabular educational prediction tasks, gradient boosting methods may provide comparable performance with reduced hyperparameter sensitivity and shorter training times. However, neural networks offer distinct advantages in scenarios requiring large-scale deployment, real-time inference, or integration into broader deep learning pipelines that process multimodal data (e.g., combining structured tabular features with unstructured text from student essays or temporal sequences from learning management system activity logs).
The progressive data enrichment analysis provides actionable guidance for institutions designing early warning systems: deploy Stage 1 models for initial risk screening at enrollment, refine predictions with Stage 2 mid-semester models to target intensive interventions, and leverage Stage 3 models for comprehensive end-of-term assessment and retention planning. This multi-stage approach balances competing imperatives of early intervention against prediction accuracy, enabling institutions to allocate support resources efficiently across the student lifecycle. Future research should explore cost-sensitive learning approaches that explicitly optimize for recall on the dropout class, advanced architectures such as attention mechanisms that could identify which features drive predictions for individual students, and transfer learning strategies that enable models trained at one institution to generalize to others with limited retraining data.

Student dropout in higher education undermines institutional missions and negatively impacts student outcomes. When students leave programs prematurely, they face diminished career prospects while often carrying substantial debt. Developing accurate predictive models enables institutions to identify at-risk students early, facilitating timely interventions.
This analysis applies feedforward artificial neural networks to predict student course completion using a dataset enriched across three temporal stages. Stage 1 includes demographic profiles and enrollment metrics. Stage 2 incorporates mid-semester performance including attendance patterns (transformed from continuous absence counts into categorical bins) and assessment outcomes. This progressive enrichment mirrors real-world data availability timelines, enabling evaluation of prediction accuracy at different intervention windows.
The work systematically evaluates neural network architectures with 1 through 9 hidden layers, maintaining 64 neurons per layer with ReLU activations, dropout regularization, and L2 weight penalties. Multiple optimization algorithms (Adam, RMSprop) are compared with learning rates 0.001-0.01 and batch sizes 32-128. Early stopping monitors validation loss with patience windows of 10-15 epochs. Results demonstrate validation accuracies exceeding 94% on Stage 3 data, with optimal performance at 5 hidden layers. Critically, performance plateaus or deteriorates beyond this depth, with 7-9 layer networks showing inferior validation accuracy despite comparable training accuracy, suggesting an optimal balance between representational capacity and generalization for educational datasets of 10,000-15,000 records.

Goals and Objectives
The primary objectives of this analysis are:

Evaluate Neural Network Architectural Complexity: Systematically assess the performance of feedforward neural networks with varying depths (1-9 hidden layers) for predicting student course completion.
